name: Gastric bypass (Roux-en-Y)

lead: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass produces some of the largest and most lasting weight loss available, which people in hardmaxx circles see as the route to a dramatically leaner body and face. Large series report loss of roughly 65 to 80 percent of excess body weight.

The stomach is divided into a small pouch and the small intestine is rearranged into a Y, so food bypasses most of the stomach and the first part of the small intestine. Gut hormone changes, eating behavior and energy expenditure all appear to contribute. It is one of the best-studied weight-loss operations, with research on obesity-related disease such as type 2 diabetes, rather than on cosmetic leaning.

paras: It is done as an operation in hospital, followed by staged diets, vitamin and mineral supplementation and lifelong nutritional follow-up. Weight loss continues over many months. Clinical eligibility is set by BMI and health conditions, not appearance; the 1991 NIH criteria are a BMI of 40 or more, or 35 or more with comorbidities.

It is major abdominal surgery. Reported complications include leaks at the joins, ulcers, strictures, dumping syndrome, bowel obstruction, internal hernia, blood clots and deficiencies in iron, calcium, B12 and thiamine. Lifelong supplements and monitoring are needed. People outside the medical criteria generally do not qualify.

angle.text: Discussed in hardmaxx circles as the most powerful route to large weight loss and the leaner body and face that follow. Research covers severe obesity and its related diseases; cosmetic leaning is not what the studies address.

lead: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) is a bariatric operation in which the stomach is divided into a small upper pouch, typically about 15 to 30 mL, and a larger remnant; the small intestine is then rearranged into a Y so that food bypasses most of the stomach and the duodenum [1]. It is performed for severe obesity and its complications, and it is one of the best-studied weight-loss operations. The Roux-en-Y reconstruction itself is named for the surgeon César Roux and is also used in operations for stomach cancer, bile-duct disease and pancreatic surgery [2].

The appearance payoff is large, sustained weight loss: it changes body composition and proportions, and the face, neck and body slim as weight falls. Large series report loss of roughly 65 to 80 percent of excess body weight, and Wikipedia reports improvement or resolution of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, sleep apnea and reflux in many patients [1]. A meta-analysis of the literature published in JAMA in 2004 examined weight loss, operative mortality and four comorbidities [3], and the Swedish Obese Subjects study reported lower overall mortality in the surgery group than in controls [4]. Large weight loss can leave excess skin, for which body-contouring plastic surgery on the arms, abdomen, thighs, buttocks and breasts is an option [5].

Clinical eligibility is set by weight and health status, not by appearance. Guidelines issued in 2022 by the American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery and the International Federation for the Surgery of Obesity and Metabolic Disorders widened the earlier 1991 NIH criteria [5]. In the looksmaxxing context the procedure is sometimes listed among hardmaxx options for dramatic weight change, which is a different use from the medical indication.

paras: The surgeon creates a small gastric pouch and connects it directly to a limb of small intestine (the Roux limb, typically 80 to 150 cm), so ingested food bypasses the remnant stomach and the duodenum. In the proximal version, the more common form in the United States, less intestine is bypassed; a distal version, with the Y-connection 100 to 150 cm from the end of the small bowel, bypasses more and causes more malabsorption and weight loss [1].

Laparoscopic RYGB was first reported in 1993 to 1994, with Wittgrove and Clark exploring it from 1993, and Rutledge developed the mini-gastric bypass in 1997 [1]. The learning curve for laparoscopic bariatric surgery is put at about 100 cases [1]. Related operations include sleeve gastrectomy, duodenal switch, the adjustable gastric band and one-anastomosis gastric bypass; Wikipedia's bariatric surgery article says sleeve gastrectomy overtook gastric bypass as the most common US procedure around 2013 [5].

Variants include the proximal and distal forms, the mini-gastric bypass (about 15 percent of Asian weight-loss operations in 2005 to 2009), and banded bypass, in which a ring is placed around the pouch outlet; banded and non-banded bypass have been compared in registered trials [1][6]. One-anastomosis gastric bypass and the SADI-S operation have been compared with RYGB in systematic reviews and randomized trials [7][8][9]. Revisional procedures exist for weight regain or insufficient weight loss after RYGB [10].

A 1991 NIH consensus panel set eligibility at a BMI of 40 or higher, or 35 or higher with at least one obesity-related comorbidity, and expects failed sustained weight loss through diet. A 2004 consensus conference of the American Society for Bariatric Surgery endorsed laparoscopic surgery and multidisciplinary preoperative evaluation [1]. Clinical guidelines for obesity care from the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and American College of Endocrinology also address surgical options [11].

In October 2022 the ASMBS and IFSO issued updated guidance recommending surgery for adults with a BMI above 35 regardless of obesity-related conditions, above 30 with metabolic syndrome, and above 27.5 in Asian populations [5]. Depression, anxiety, eating disorders and substance use are reported more often in people with severe obesity, and depressive symptoms generally decrease after surgery [5].

The 2004 JAMA meta-analysis evaluated weight loss, operative mortality and obesity comorbidities including diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertension and sleep apnea, and concluded the operation generally led to improvement of these [3]. A 2009 meta-analysis reported on weight and type 2 diabetes after bariatric surgery [12]. Randomized trials comparing bariatric surgery with intensive medical therapy in people with type 2 diabetes have reported greater glycemic control with surgery, including five-year results from a trial of RYGB and sleeve gastrectomy [13][14].

Wikipedia reports diabetes reversal in up to 90 percent of patients in some series, hyperlipidemia and hypertension corrected in over 70 percent, and a 2021 Lancet meta-analysis of 174,772 participants finding lower mortality after bariatric surgery in obese adults with and without diabetes [1]. The Swedish Obese Subjects study, a prospective controlled study of 4,047 people, compared surgery with conventional care for overall mortality, and a companion study of long-term mortality after gastric bypass appeared in the same journal issue [4][15].

Randomized trials comparing sleeve gastrectomy with RYGB include SM-BOSS and SLEEVEPASS, with five-year and longer follow-up published in JAMA and JAMA Surgery; meta-analyses of the trials examine long-term outcomes [16][17][18][19][20][21]. Wikipedia's bariatric surgery article summarises five-year data as greater weight loss after bypass than sleeve (26 versus 19 percent) with a lower rate of diabetes relapse, but more hospitalizations and further abdominal surgery in the bypass group [5].

The main visible effect is weight loss, with a gradual change in body shape over months to years. Wikipedia's bariatric surgery article notes that excess skin may form after major weight loss and that body-contouring operations for the arms, buttocks, thighs, abdomen and breasts may be considered, with changes occurring slowly over years; it adds that follow-up body lifts and liposuction carry added risks, especially when nutritional deficiencies are present [1][5].

Hair loss is listed among the consequences of protein malnutrition after the operation [1]. Muscle weakness from reduced protein intake is another reported effect [1]. Depressive symptoms generally decrease after surgery, and body image and self-esteem often improve, according to the same article [5]. None of the cited trials was designed to measure facial appearance, and no study found specifically examines facial changes after RYGB.

Wikipedia gives 30-day complication rates of about 7 percent for laparoscopic and 14.5 percent for open surgery, with 30-day mortality of about 0.11 percent in US accredited-center data. Reported complications include anastomotic leak (about 2 percent), anastomotic ulcers (1 to 16 percent), strictures, dumping syndrome, internal hernia (about 0.2 percent), bowel obstruction, bleeding and venous thromboembolism [1]. A systematic review has examined the prevalence and pathophysiology of dumping syndrome after bariatric surgery [22]. Gallstones (roughly 3 to 13 percent) and kidney stones (roughly 7 to 11 percent) are also reported after bypass [5].

Nutritional deficiencies are common and can be under-recognized: calcium and iron (because the duodenum is bypassed), vitamin B12, thiamine, folate, zinc, fat-soluble vitamins and protein. Thiamine deficiency can cause Wernicke's encephalopathy, and one study cited by Wikipedia found deficiencies went unrecognized in about half of patients. Other reported effects include lower alcohol tolerance, with a small study finding higher and longer-lasting breath alcohol than in controls, and post-operative depression [1]. A meta-analysis has examined short-term bone density changes after RYGB or sleeve [23]. Wikipedia notes that alcohol is avoided completely for the first 6 to 12 months after surgery [5].

Weight loss was traditionally attributed to restriction and malabsorption. Later research points to hormonal and behavioral changes. A study in the New England Journal of Medicine compared plasma ghrelin after diet-induced weight loss and after gastric bypass [24], and work in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences examined gut microbiota in obesity and after bypass [25]. Gut hormones such as CCK, PYY and GLP-1 are involved, while ghrelin is reduced; a rat study found increased energy expenditure after the operation. The full mechanism is debated [1].

Before 1991, severe obesity was defined as at least 100 pounds above an actuarial ideal weight; that year an NIH consensus panel set the BMI-based criteria still widely cited [1]. Laparoscopic RYGB was reported in 1993 to 1994 [1]. A 1995 report in Annals of Surgery described the operation as the most effective treatment for adult-onset diabetes mellitus, an early landmark in the metabolic-surgery literature [26]. Rutledge's mini-gastric bypass followed in 1997, and in 2007 the New England Journal of Medicine published two mortality studies [1][4][15]. About 140,000 gastric bypass procedures were performed in the US in 2005 and about 200,000 in 2008 per Wikipedia's figures [1][5].

Human studies include randomized trials comparing bariatric surgery with intensive medical therapy for type 2 diabetes [13][14], large prospective controlled studies of mortality [4][15], and systematic reviews and meta-analyses of weight loss and comorbidities [3][12]. Registered trials include comparisons of banded and non-banded RYGB and of RYGB versus one-anastomosis gastric bypass [6][7]. These studies enroll patients with medical obesity; none was designed to test cosmetic or facial outcomes.

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing-adjacent discussion RYGB is mentioned as a hardmaxx route to major weight change; the claims below are those made in the clinical and patient-advocacy literature, with the expert record beside them.

claims.claim: Gastric bypass produces large, lasting weight loss.
Weight loss works by physically limiting stomach size.
Gastric bypass is a cosmetic shortcut to a leaner face and body.
Rapid weight loss leaves loose skin that may need further surgery.
Vitamin and mineral deficiencies are a known lifelong risk.

timeline.event: NIH consensus panel sets criteria for bariatric surgery: BMI 40 or higher, or 35 or higher with comorbidity [1].
Laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass first performed [1].
Annals of Surgery report highlights diabetes remission after gastric bypass [26].
NEJM study compares plasma ghrelin after diet-induced weight loss and after gastric bypass [24].
JAMA meta-analysis of bariatric surgery outcomes; ASBS consensus conference updates criteria [1][3].
Swedish Obese Subjects and a long-term gastric bypass mortality study report lower mortality after bariatric surgery [4][15].
NEJM trial of bariatric surgery versus intensive medical therapy for diabetes [14].
SM-BOSS and SLEEVEPASS trials report sleeve versus RYGB weight loss [19][20].
Lancet meta-analysis of 174,772 participants reports lower mortality after bariatric surgery [1].
ASMBS/IFSO guidance widens eligibility to BMI above 35 regardless of conditions [5].
